scope: Tactically meaningful fork attributable to the exact recorded move, with two non-pawn targets. Single blinded review of board and Stockfish branches.

cases.rationale: Qxf4 wins the forking pawn and preserves the knight.
Nxb4 exchanges the forker at no material cost; the other attacked piece escapes.
Nxf7+ wins via Qxe5 or a mating attack after Rxf7. The separate value of the threat to h6 is unclear.
Qxc3 meets the double attack with an even queen exchange.
Rxa7 trades rooks and does not retain the attacked knight.
Qc3 or Qd2 preserves material. The later Bxf3 is an even exchange.
Qe1 allows an equal queen exchange without losing either original target.
Either rook captures the queen and avoids a profitable second arm.
Nf6 saves the knight and Qf4 offers an even queen exchange. The piece on f8 never falls for a gain.
Nxf6+ is recaptured after Rfc8; Nxd7 instead permits Rxd7 and Rxd5. The second arm has unclear net value.
Best defence Nxa6 removes the forker and avoids material loss; Kc8 would lose the knight.
Qb3 initiates a favourable queen exchange before either target can be won.
Bf8 avoids Qxg7, which wins after Kd7. The best blocking reply leaves the relevance of the rook threat unclear.
Nf3+ may induce Nxd4, but best separate Kh1 uses Nfh4 and leaves the second arm unresolved.
Qxf5 pivots to b1 promotion. Nd2 allows Qxb1 and the rook reply. How much the attacks on f3 and d5 matter is unclear.
Rxf2+ gives up the fork piece to reach b7 by either capture. The actual fork targets do not drive the pawn race.
Rxf8+ is the counterattack. Neither e3 nor b6 is won at a material profit in the principal replies.
Promotion gives check and attacks a8. Kh7 allows Qxa8; Rxd8 gives up a rook to Rxd8+.
Bxa7 or Nxd5 avoids an effective collection of c3 or e3.
Bxc4 exchanges the fork piece; Qf2 allows Nxe3 Qxe3. The trade may have positional value, but no retained fork payoff is clear.
Rxe8 by the other rook is an even exchange. Bf8 concedes that rook, but is substantially weaker.
Qxf7 interrupts the queen's attack and does not concede the two original targets.
Qxg7 forces an exchange without losing the attacked minor pieces.
Rxf3+ trades off the attacker without paying for either threatened target.
Nb6+ displaces the king and collects the rook on d7. Kb8 requires Nxd7+ Nxd7; Kc7 allows a further capture on f8.
Rxd2 or Kxd2 removes the rook without material gain from the original targets.
Qxe2 and Bxe2 remove the knight. No other attacked piece is lost.
Ne5+ checks the king and attacks g4. Kd8 and Ke8 both allow Nxg4.
Rxg2+ escapes the king's apparent double attack and gives Black the winning initiative.
Qxf5 and Rxf5 exchange queens; Ke2 allows a worse direct capture but is unnecessary.
Rxf7 and Kxf7 take the forking rook. The compensating activity is elsewhere.
The best continuations after Qxe3+ are Qg5 and Bg6. The suggested threat of Qxd2 is not established as a separately profitable branch.
Qxb2 Bxb2 exchanges the fork piece; the c1 rook survives.
Bd4+ attacks c5 and the king. Both king moves allow Bxc5 for an exchange gain even if Nxc5 follows.
Rd1+ induces a queen concession with Qe1, but the explicit c1 rook attack is not collected by the best lines.
Bxf7 trades bishops off; the line where Kg7 allows Bxe6 is an avoidable loss.
Nd5 saves the knight, and Nxf6 Bxf6 in the c3 line is an even exchange.
Qxc8 or Qc2 trades queens. The check does not win a second target.
Nxd4 Bxd4 is an ordinary knight exchange with no retained second arm.
Bxe5 neutralizes the forker and the Rxd7 recapture sequence loses material; the checkless counterattack also survives.
exd5 removes the knight and entirely prevents collection of the original targets.
Qxd6 Rxd6 is an equal exchange; the alternative Qxb6 trades queens as well.
Qxd1+ has already made its root capture. Bf1 permits Qxf3 but Kh2 plans b4 and no capture of f3.
Rxd6 removes the queen without losing either rook. Qxd8 in the second line does not make the fork unavoidable.
The actual fork develops at Ne6 in both replies. Rxf8+ clears the way.
Bxg7+ is a sacrifice to expose the king. Kxg7 is forced in the search and removed the alleged fork piece.
Qxe5 Rxe5 is an even exchange; Qxc3 Nxc3 is the same liquidation.
Best Qxe4 dxe4 trades queens. The knight attack never secures a gain against it.
Nxd4 or coordinated rook defence neutralises the double attack without losing material.
The two independent replies lead to Qh6 and Rxe4. The route via Nxg8 may be relevant, but the original c8 and d5 targets lack a clean payoff.
Neither b4 nor Nfd2 concedes a material capture of an original target.
Rxd8 removes the forker with an even exchange. The queen capture alternative keeps the struggle on other squares.
g5 offers an equal queen exchange and Ne5 addresses the other queen retreat. The fork wins no target.
Either recapture removes the forking rook. The later Nxe8 is a distinct action.
Rxc4 removes the overextended queen. Re1 allows a much worse queen-for-rook trade but is avoidable.
Rc7 puts pressure on f7 and b7, but after best Raf8 the gain comes on a7 instead. Other candidate captures trade rooks.
Qxc7 gives the opponent a rook and counters Bxa8. The resulting exchange falls well below the better root evaluation.
Re4 and Qb1 or Nf4 coordinate the targets without losing material.
Nxb6 and Rxb6 both remove the queen with no profitable remaining attack by it.
Rf6 and Rb6 remove the attacked rook. Neither line wins the other target through the attacked rook's move.
dxe4 wins the tactical initiative and neutralizes the knight, leaving none of the apparent targets lost.
Rf4 allows Nxh2 but Rhxh2 replies, while Nxg4 is also sound. The precise value of the double attack is unclear.
Queen retreats save the queen and the knight stays soundly defended.
Qxd4+ cxd4 trades queens even under the check. Kg2 gives concessions by choice.
